questions.question: Why does Bassanio seek Antonio’s financial help at the beginning?

options.text: To compete with Portia’s wealthy suitors at Belmont.
To buy back Jessica’s stolen jewels from Tubal.
To pay the fine imposed on Shylock in court.
To finance Lorenzo’s return from Belmont.

questions.explanation: Bassanio wants the means to present himself as a rival for Portia’s hand.

evidence.exact:
BASSANIO.
In Belmont is a lady richly left,
And she is fair, and, fairer than that word,
Of wondrous virtues. Sometimes from her eyes
I did receive fair speechless messages:
Her name is Portia, nothing undervalu’d
To Cato’s daughter, Brutus’ Portia.
Nor is the wide world ignorant of her worth,
For the four winds blow in from every coast
Renowned suitors, and her sunny locks
Hang on her temples like a golden fleece,
Which makes her seat of Belmont Colchos’ strond,
And many Jasons come in quest of her.
O my Antonio, had I but the means
To hold a rival place with one of them,
I have a mind presages me such thrift
That I should questionless be fortunate.

questions.question: What penalty does Shylock’s bond specify if Antonio fails to repay on time?

options.text: All of Bassanio’s inheritance.
A pound of Antonio’s flesh.
Portia’s marriage ring.
Half of Lorenzo’s estate.

questions.explanation: The bond names a pound of Antonio’s flesh as the forfeit for nonpayment.

evidence.exact:
SHYLOCK.
This kindness will I show.
Go with me to a notary, seal me there
Your single bond; and in a merry sport,
If you repay me not on such a day,
In such a place, such sum or sums as are
Express’d in the condition, let the forfeit
Be nominated for an equal pound
Of your fair flesh, to be cut off and taken
In what part of your body pleaseth me.

questions.question: What limits Portia’s freedom to choose a husband?

options.text: The Duke of Venice must approve every suitor.
Antonio must first repay the loan to Shylock.
Her father’s will requires the suitor to choose the right casket.
Nerissa has promised her to the Prince of Morocco.

questions.explanation: Portia says her dead father’s will governs her choice, and Nerissa explains the three-casket test.

evidence.exact:
PORTIA.
If to do were as easy as to know what were good to do, chapels had been churches, and poor men’s cottages princes’ palaces. It is a good divine that follows his own instructions; I can easier teach twenty what were good to be done than to be one of the twenty to follow mine own teaching. The brain may devise laws for the blood, but a hot temper leaps o’er a cold decree; such a hare is madness the youth, to skip o’er the meshes of good counsel the cripple. But this reasoning is not in the fashion to choose me a husband. O me, the word “choose”! I may neither choose who I would nor refuse who I dislike, so is the will of a living daughter curb’d by the will of a dead father. Is it not hard, Nerissa, that I cannot choose one, nor refuse none?
evidence.prefix: ld be better if well followed.

evidence.exact:
NERISSA.
Your father was ever virtuous, and holy men at their death have good inspirations. Therefore the lott’ry that he hath devised in these three chests of gold, silver, and lead, whereof who chooses his meaning chooses you, will no doubt never be chosen by any rightly but one who you shall rightly love. But what warmth is there in your affection towards any of these princely suitors that are already come?
evidence.prefix: t choose one, nor refuse none?

questions.question: Why does Bassanio choose the lead casket?

options.text: He believes gold represents the plainest and most honest choice.
He thinks silver guarantees exactly what every suitor deserves.
He follows the choice already made by Morocco.
He distrusts attractive appearances and accepts lead’s unpromising exterior.

questions.explanation: Bassanio rejects deceptive ornament and is moved by plain lead rather than gold or silver.

evidence.exact:
BASSANIO.
So may the outward shows be least themselves.
The world is still deceiv’d with ornament.
In law, what plea so tainted and corrupt
But, being season’d with a gracious voice,
Obscures the show of evil? In religion,
What damned error but some sober brow
Will bless it, and approve it with a text,
Hiding the grossness with fair ornament?
There is no vice so simple but assumes
Some mark of virtue on his outward parts.
How many cowards, whose hearts are all as false
As stairs of sand, wear yet upon their chins
The beards of Hercules and frowning Mars,
Who inward search’d, have livers white as milk,
And these assume but valour’s excrement
To render them redoubted. Look on beauty,
And you shall see ’tis purchas’d by the weight,
Which therein works a miracle in nature,
Making them lightest that wear most of it:
So are those crisped snaky golden locks
Which make such wanton gambols with the wind
Upon supposed fairness, often known
To be the dowry of a second head,
The skull that bred them in the sepulchre.
Thus ornament is but the guiled shore
To a most dangerous sea; the beauteous scarf
Veiling an Indian beauty; in a word,
The seeming truth which cunning times put on
To entrap the wisest. Therefore thou gaudy gold,
Hard food for Midas, I will none of thee,
Nor none of thee, thou pale and common drudge
’Tween man and man: but thou, thou meagre lead,
Which rather threaten’st than dost promise aught,
Thy palenness moves me more than eloquence,
And here choose I, joy be the consequence!

questions.question: What future does Jessica plan with Lorenzo?

options.text: Leave her father’s household, become Christian, and marry Lorenzo.
Remain with Shylock while Lorenzo marries Nerissa.
Travel to Padua to study law with Bellario.
Persuade Lorenzo to enforce Antonio’s bond.

questions.explanation: Jessica anticipates ending her conflict with her father by becoming Lorenzo’s wife and adopting his faith.

evidence.exact:
Alack, what heinous sin is it in me
To be ashamed to be my father’s child!
But though I am a daughter to his blood,
I am not to his manners. O Lorenzo,
If thou keep promise, I shall end this strife,
Become a Christian and thy loving wife.

questions.question: How does Shylock explain his desire to take Antonio’s flesh?

options.text: As a way to secure Portia’s choice of the silver casket.
As revenge for Antonio’s insults and injuries against him.
As repayment for Lorenzo’s purchase of a ship.
As a reward promised by Bellario for serving the court.

questions.explanation: Shylock describes Antonio’s mistreatment and says the flesh will feed his revenge.

evidence.exact:
SHYLOCK.
To bait fish withal; if it will feed nothing else, it will feed my revenge. He hath disgrac’d me and hind’red me half a million, laugh’d at my losses, mock’d at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my bargains, cooled my friends, heated mine enemies. And what’s his reason? I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? Fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is? If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge? If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in that. If a Jew wrong a Christian, what is his humility? Revenge. If a Christian wrong a Jew, what should his sufferance be by Christian example? Why, revenge! The villainy you teach me I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction.
evidence.prefix: s flesh! What’s that good for?
evidence.suffix:
Enter a man from Antonio.

SER

questions.question: What role has Portia secretly performed before revealing herself at Belmont?

options.text: The Duke who presided over the Venetian court.
The messenger who brought news of Jessica’s flight.
The learned doctor who judged the bond dispute.
The clerk who accompanied Nerissa to court.

questions.explanation: Bellario’s letter identifies Portia as the doctor and Nerissa as her clerk.

evidence.exact:
PORTIA.
Speak not so grossly. You are all amaz’d.
Here is a letter; read it at your leisure.
It comes from Padua from Bellario.
There you shall find that Portia was the doctor,
Nerissa there, her clerk. Lorenzo here
Shall witness I set forth as soon as you,
And even but now return’d. I have not yet
Enter’d my house. Antonio, you are welcome,
And I have better news in store for you
Than you expect: unseal this letter soon.
There you shall find three of your argosies
Are richly come to harbour suddenly.
You shall not know by what strange accident
I chanced on this letter.
evidence.prefix: kolds ere we have deserv’d it?

questions.question: What distinction does Portia use to stop Shylock from taking the forfeited flesh?

options.text: The bond grants blood but no flesh.
The bond expires when Bassanio marries.
The bond binds Bassanio rather than Antonio.
The bond grants flesh but no blood.

questions.explanation: Portia insists on the literal wording: a pound of flesh, with no right to shed blood.

evidence.exact:
PORTIA.
Tarry a little, there is something else.
This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood.
The words expressly are “a pound of flesh”:
Take then thy bond, take thou thy pound of flesh,
But in the cutting it, if thou dost shed
One drop of Christian blood, thy lands and goods
Are, by the laws of Venice, confiscate
Unto the state of Venice.

questions.question: What two additional conditions does Antonio demand when Shylock is spared?

options.text: Conversion to Christianity and a recorded inheritance for Lorenzo and Jessica.
Marriage to Nerissa and repayment of Bassanio’s debts.
Exile from Venice and the sale of Portia’s estate.
Return of the ring and a pardon for Bellario.

questions.explanation: Antonio requires immediate conversion and a legal gift of Shylock’s remaining estate to Lorenzo and Jessica at his death.

evidence.exact:
ANTONIO.
So please my lord the Duke and all the court
To quit the fine for one half of his goods,
I am content, so he will let me have
The other half in use, to render it
Upon his death unto the gentleman
That lately stole his daughter.
Two things provided more, that for this favour,
He presently become a Christian;
The other, that he do record a gift,
Here in the court, of all he dies possess’d
Unto his son Lorenzo and his daughter.
evidence.suffix:
DUKE.
He shall do this, or els

questions.question: Why does Bassanio finally give the doctor the ring he promised Portia to keep?

options.text: Portia openly releases him from the promise before the court.
Antonio urges him to value the doctor’s service and their friendship above the promise.
Shylock makes the ring a condition of abandoning the bond.
Lorenzo tells him the ring originally belonged to Jessica.

questions.explanation: Bassanio first cites his promise, then yields after Antonio appeals to the doctor’s merits and his own love.

evidence.exact:
BASSANIO.
Good sir, this ring was given me by my wife,
And when she put it on, she made me vow
That I should neither sell, nor give, nor lose it.
evidence.prefix: w a beggar should be answer’d.

evidence.exact:
ANTONIO.
My Lord Bassanio, let him have the ring.
Let his deservings and my love withal
Be valued ’gainst your wife’s commandment.

BASSANIO.
Go, Gratiano, run and overtake him;
Give him the ring, and bring him if thou canst
Unto Antonio’s house. Away, make haste.
